title: Occasion and date
short: Written in 1902 from a conversation with Maud Gonne and her sister Kathleen Pilcher, shortly before Gonne married John MacBride (1903).
body: The poem recalls an evening on which Yeats talked with Maud Gonne ('you') and her sister Kathleen Pilcher ('That beautiful mild woman your close friend'). It was published in the Monthly Review in December 1902 and collected in In the Seven Woods (Dun Emer Press, 1903), and was written just before Gonne's marriage to John MacBride in February 1903, a blow Yeats felt deeply. The poem is usually taken to draw on a real meeting of the three; Yeats alters the situation slightly, turning the sister into Gonne's 'close friend'.

title: Couplets and conversation
short: Heroic couplets, often slant-rhymed and heavily enjambed, give the poem the ease of talk; the first paragraph is a 14-line quasi-sonnet.
body: The poem is in pentameter couplets, but Yeats loosens them: rhymes are sometimes full (thought/naught, bones/stones), sometimes partial (enough/love, school/beautiful), and sentences run on across line and paragraph breaks. The first verse paragraph runs fourteen lines, suggesting a sonnet, and ends on a short line ('The martyrs call the world') completed by the start of the next ('That woman then'). The effect enacts the poem's argument: what looks like casual speech is the result of labour. The movement from argument to silence ('We sat grown quiet') to private confession gives the poem a three-part structure.

title: a moment's thought
greek: Italian sprezzatura; Latin ars est celare artem
short: A line of verse may take hours, but must appear spontaneous: art that hides its art.
body: The poet's first claim is that labour must be concealed: a line 'will take us hours maybe', but if it does not 'seem a moment's thought' the work is wasted. This is the classical ideal that art should conceal art (Latin ars est celare artem) and the Renaissance courtier's sprezzatura, the studied ease described in Castiglione's Book of the Courtier, a work Yeats came to admire. 'Us' makes the poet speak for poets in general. The idea underlies the whole poem: the beauty of verse, of women, and of courtly love are all achieved through hidden effort.

title: stitching and unstitching
short: Composition as needlework, sewn and unpicked; the domestic image links the poet's labour to women's work.
body: The poet compares revising a line to sewing and unpicking a seam, a domestic and traditionally female craft. The image prepares Kathleen's reply that women too 'must labour to be beautiful'. Readers may also hear Penelope in the Odyssey, who weaves by day and unpicks by night, though the phrase does not require the allusion. 'Naught', nothing, is a slightly archaic word that gives the line weight.

title: go down upon your marrow bones
short: Colloquial for 'on your knees', as for scrubbing a floor.
body: 'Marrow bones' is a jocular or colloquial term for the knees; 'to go down on one's marrow-bones' means to kneel, as here to scrub a kitchen floor. The OED records the phrase in English from the early modern period. The homely idiom brings physical drudgery into a poem about refined art, and the comparison argues that verse is harder than manual labour. 'Pavement' here means a paved floor.

title: break stones / Like an old pauper
short: Stone-breaking was the classic task set to paupers in Victorian workhouses and on the roads.
body: Breaking stones for roads was the archetypal hard labour of the poor: workhouses and relief schemes in Britain and Ireland set able-bodied paupers to it as a 'labour test'. The 'old pauper in all kinds of weather' is the lowest image of toil the poet can find, and verse is said to be harder still. The comparison is partly playful exaggeration, part of the poem's 'mock-serious' tone noted by critics, and partly serious about a poet's unseen effort.

title: articulate
short: 'Articulate' keeps its root sense of joining: verse fits sounds together as joints are fitted.
body: From Latin articulus, a small joint, 'articulate' means to join, and then to utter distinctly. Here both senses work: to write verse is to fit 'sweet sounds together' as a craftsman joins pieces, and so to make them speak. The phrase is itself a line in which sound is carefully composed. It sums up the poet's labour in a single elevated verb after the plain list of scrubbing and stone-breaking.

title: The martyrs call the world
short: The worldly crowd of bankers, schoolmasters and clergymen are what martyrs call 'the world'; the poet aligns himself with the martyrs.
body: The 'noisy set / Of bankers, schoolmasters, and clergymen' are the respectable and practical people who think the poet an 'idler'. Yeats calls them what the martyrs call 'the world', using the New Testament sense of the world as the sphere of worldliness opposed to the spirit (as in 1 John 2:15, 'Love not the world'). The poet thus implies that artists are martyrs, suffering for a higher calling; the Wikipedia summary notes that the speaker aligns himself with the martyrs and speaks from a victim's standpoint. The inclusion of 'clergymen' is a sly twist: the clergy themselves belong to 'the world'. The joke is half serious.

title: That beautiful mild woman
short: Kathleen Pilcher, Maud Gonne's sister, presented as 'your close friend'; her mildness and youth are stressed.
body: The 'beautiful mild woman' is usually identified as Kathleen Pilcher (née Gonne), Maud's younger sister. The poem calls her 'your close friend', not sister, a small alteration of fact. Later the poet says that many 'shall find out all heartache' for her 'mild sake', in finding her voice 'young and mild and low', a phrase that recalls King Lear's praise of Cordelia's voice, 'ever soft, / Gentle, and low' (5.3), a possible echo. Kathleen's mildness contrasts with the fierce Maud of later poems such as 'No Second Troy'.

anchor: we must labour to be beautiful
title: we must labour to be beautiful
short: Kathleen's reply: women know without being taught that beauty takes work; the poem extends the poet's case to women's lives.
body: Kathleen answers that 'all we women know', though no school teaches it, that beauty must be laboured for. Her words widen the poem's argument: the labour of art is matched by the labour, often unacknowledged, of being beautiful. Elizabeth Butler Cullingford's essay 'Labour and Memory in the Love Poetry of W. B. Yeats' examines how the poem links poetic and feminine labour, and how both are hidden behind an appearance of ease. The poem gives women a voice in the debate but also casts beauty as a performance, which some feminist readers have questioned.

title: Adam's fall; the title
short: Labour as the curse laid on Adam (Genesis 3:17-19): since the Fall nothing fine is made without toil.
body: The title and these lines allude to Genesis 3:17-19, where God curses the ground for Adam's sake: 'in the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread'. Before the Fall, work and delight were one; afterwards, every good thing must be laboured for. The poet generalises the curse to art, beauty and love. Wikipedia's summary notes that the title evokes the Fall and the separation of work from pleasure. 'Labouring' rhymes with 'thing', giving the couplet the finality of a maxim; it is one of the most quoted statements of Yeats's aesthetic of hard-won ease.

title: high courtesy; beautiful old books
short: The courtly love tradition, in which lovers sighed by the rules found in old romances; 'precedents' treats love as law.
body: The 'lovers who thought love should be / So much compounded of high courtesy' are the courtly lovers of medieval romance and troubadour lyric, for whom love was an art with rules, refined manners and devotion to an unattainable lady. They 'quote with learned looks / Precedents out of beautiful old books', as a lawyer cites cases. Yeats had modelled his own long devotion to Gonne on this ideal, which is why the 'old high way of love' returns in the poem's last section. 'Compounded' means made up of, as of ingredients.

title: an idle trade enough
short: Courtly love now seems an idle occupation, recalling 'idler' (l. 12): the world's verdict on poets turned upon love.
body: 'Idle trade' is a near-oxymoron, a trade being a working occupation. The phrase echoes the 'idler' of l. 12: what the worldly think of poets, the poet now thinks of the courtly lovers, and by implication of his own devotion. 'Enough' here means 'sufficiently, quite', an idiomatic intensifier. The line marks the turn from argument to feeling, and the next line (l. 29), 'We sat grown quiet at the name of love', shows that the topic has touched the speakers too closely.

title: A moon, worn as if it had been a shell
short: The new moon is likened to a shell worn thin by the tides of time breaking into days and years.
body: In the dying light appears a moon 'worn as if it had been a shell / Washed by time's waters'. The thin crescent looks like a sea-shell eroded by the waves; the 'waters' are those of time, rising and falling about the stars and breaking 'in days and years', as waves break on a shore. The image transfers the theme of labour and wear from art and beauty to the cosmos: even the moon is worn down. The 'trembling blue-green' of the sky gives one of Yeats's most delicate colour effects. The moon will return in the last line (l. 39) as 'that hollow moon'.

anchor: the old high way of love
title: the old high way of love
short: The private thought addressed to Gonne: he tried to love her in the courtly manner, a devotion she repeatedly declined.
body: The last paragraph is a confession meant 'for no one's but your ears', that is, for Maud Gonne. 'The old high way of love' is the courtly ideal of the previous paragraph, now applied to Yeats's own devotion. He had proposed marriage to Gonne several times from 1891 onward and been refused; within weeks of the poem's publication she married MacBride. The sentence moves in three clauses ('That you were beautiful ... That I strove ... That it had all seemed happy'), each a little sadder, and ends with the image of the moon.

title: that hollow moon
short: The lovers have grown as weary and empty as the worn moon; the poem ends on a slant rhyme of 'grown' and 'moon'.
body: The worn, shell-like moon of ll. 32-34 now becomes 'hollow', an image of the lovers' hearts emptied by long effort. The final couplet's slant rhyme ('grown' / 'moon') leaves the poem slightly unresolved, in keeping with a love that has not been answered. The moon was already one of Yeats's favourite symbols and would later become central to his system in A Vision (1925). Here it serves a simple, poignant purpose: even beauty and love, like the moon, wear away.
